title: Hazel and the Borrowed Umbrella
markdown:
Hazel lived in a cosy house by a cricket field, a whirlwind of fur who wanted more from a night than acorns. Mr Buttons the teddy preferred naps. Clover the bunny considered a fresh dandelion a reasonable thrill. Days were gentle: games, rest, the window humming with a world that did not come in.

Every day Hazel’s paws itched anyway.

Until one night the child’s breathing deepened into true sleep. Hazel’s eyes caught. “Psst.” She nudged the bear. “The hazel copse. And I know what we need.” Tail toward the garden shed. “Mairwen Badger’s umbrella. She never returns things, so woodland law says it is practically ours.”

Because of that, a plan with mischief in it. Quiet as shadows, back door, a breeze for a latch. The moon a silver coin, inky fingers on dew. Crickets hushed as if they had tickets. At the copse edge: old earth, secrets. “Mairwen’s sett is past that grumpy oak.”

A deep grumpy voice. “Halt. Purpose, intruders.” Ferdinand the toad occupied a teacup on a twisted root, a throne the size of a sip. Obsidian eyes. “We need Mairwen’s umbrella,” Mr Buttons stammered, hugging Clover.

“Need is not ownership. Mairwen owns it. You do not. Therefore you cannot need it. Simple.”

Clover’s ears drooped. Hazel rolled her eyes. “What if we borrow it and leave something better for when she wakes?”

Ferdinand’s throat pulsed. “Borrowing implies return. If you replace it with better, she loses nothing. That is fair.”

Mr Buttons saw the gap. “A dandelion clock.” Clover bounced. “Three shiny pebbles.” Hazel, impatient in the useful way, nudged the grand green umbrella free. Fabric dripped dew. “Quickly.”

With the green umbrella dripping dew, they did not flee the copse. They ran toward Mairwen’s sett, moonlight turning the floor to mosaic, to complete the fairness Ferdinand had defined. They found plump red strawberries that smelled of stored sunshine and set them by the entrance. Hazel added juicy dark blackberries. The forest floor, damp, whispering, felt alive with the silent gift. A soft snuffle nearby: Mairwen stirring. “Time to go,” Hazel hissed, heart thumping. The woods felt friendlier, the exchange a promise rather than a raid.

Until finally they were home, three heartbeats in a pile, the umbrella’s absence from the shed already someone else’s morning problem, the fruit standing in for canvas at a badger’s door.

Ever since then, when the moon found the leaves, Hazel’s itch remembered the thrill of an adventure that left someone better off — even a badger with a habit of not returning things. Clover dreamed dandelions. Mr Buttons, against his own nap policy, stayed awake just long enough to be proud.
characters: Hazel (squirrel whose paws itch for more than acorns), Mr Buttons (a teddy who prefers naps), Clover (a bunny thrilled by dandelions)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
